title: Akshay Kumar and Priyadarshan Waited 16 Years to Make You Scream-Laugh Again. Bhooth Bangla Just Hit Netflix.
excerpt: A ₹163-crore haunted-house hit, a wedding where no bride is supposed to survive, and the comedy duo that built your childhood — streaming now, anywhere in the world.
body:
The doors of the cursed mansion swing open, the lights flicker, Akshay Kumar grabs a torch like it's a weapon, and somewhere in the dark a ghost is already laughing harder than the audience. That's the opening promise of **Bhooth Bangla**, and after a 16-year drought, it's the promise we'd almost stopped expecting.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=sL7V1INn6io</youtube>

Because this is the reunion. **Akshay Kumar** and director **Priyadarshan** — the partnership that gave the diaspora *Hera Pheri*, *Garam Masala*, *Bhagam Bhag*, *Bhool Bhulaiyaa* — hadn't shared a set since *Khatta Meetha* in 2010. For a generation of NRIs who grew up rewinding VHS tapes and quoting Babu Bhaiya at family dinners, their split felt like a band breaking up. *Bhooth Bangla* is them getting back together, plugging the amps back in, and turning the volume to chaos.

> The film began streaming on Netflix from 12 June 2026. — Wikipedia



> **"No theatrical-window math, no piracy guilt, no "wait for the DVD that's never coming." Just press play."**


That's the headline for everyone reading this from a flat in London, a townhouse in Toronto, or an apartment in New Jersey: it's on **Netflix now**, globally, in Hindi. No theatrical-window math, no piracy guilt, no "wait for the DVD that's never coming." Just press play.

The setup is pure Priyadarshan: **Arjun Acharya** (Akshay), a financially drowning man in London, inherits a sprawling palace in a small Indian town. Naturally, he decides to host his sister's long-delayed wedding there. There's only one problem — local legend swears that no bride survives in the town. The mansion groans, apparitions drift through corridors, and Arjun, equal parts ghostbuster and grifter, has to keep a wedding running while the dead keep crashing it. It is exactly the kind of premise this director has been weaponizing for laughs his entire career.


![Akshay Kumar — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2a/Akshay_Kumar_National_Award_for_Padman_%28cropped%29.jpg)


And the ensemble is a roll call of faces the diaspora loves. **Tabu**, luminous and unsettling in the same breath. **Paresh Rawal** and **Rajpal Yadav**, the comic engine room. **Wamiqa Gabbi**, **Mithila Palkar**, **Jisshu Sengupta**, **Sharman Joshi** — and, in one of his final screen appearances, the beloved **Asrani**, whose presence gives the whole thing a bittersweet undertow nobody saw coming.

Let's be honest about the reviews, because a knowing friend tells you the truth. They were mixed. *Bollywood Hungama* was warmest at 3.5 stars, calling it "a fair entertainer that works best for its humour, performances and old-school Priyadarshan-style chaos," while flagging a second half that "loses some steam." *The Times of India* landed at 3, praising a "thoroughly entertaining" first half before the screenplay "turns messy." *India Today* and *Deccan Herald* were cooler at 2.5, the latter delivering the sharpest line of the lot: the film "has all the teeth, but unfortunately none of the bite."

So it's not vintage *Hera Pheri*. The back half drifts, the climax overstays, and the creature work occasionally tips into gimmick. But here's what the star ratings missed — audiences didn't care. They showed up, and they kept showing up.

> Bhooth Bangla has emerged as a hit, with collections of over Rs 150 crore.

The film crossed **₹163 crore net in India** and was *still* adding collections deep into its seventh week — a 48-day theatrical leg that most 2026 releases would kill for. In an era where films evaporate from cinemas in a fortnight, a horror-comedy with "messy" reviews holding the box office for nearly two months tells you something the critics didn't: people wanted to laugh in a crowd again, and they wanted Akshay and Priyadarshan to be the ones making them.

That's the real diaspora pitch here. *Bhooth Bangla* isn't trying to be prestige cinema. It's a Friday-night, family-on-the-couch, everyone-talking-over-the-screen kind of film — the comfort food of a very specific Indian childhood, served hot on the world's biggest streaming platform. If you've got cousins coming over, a long weekend, and a craving for the kind of slapstick that doesn't require subtitles to land, this is your watch.

Sixteen years is a long time to wait for a sequel to a friendship. The ghosts, it turns out, were just the excuse to get the band back in the same haunted room.
